newsitem.title: GERMANY: Budget shortfalls pile pressure on Bonn coalition.
newsitem.headline: Budget shortfalls pile pressure on Bonn coalition.

text.p: Bonn's centrist Free Democrats (FDP) declared on Sunday that a bitter coalition budget spat was over, but sniping from their coalition partners and the prospect of new revenue shortfalls suggested the row was far from settled.

Last week FDP leader Wolfgang Gerhardt had threatened to quit the coalition if Finance Minister Theo Waigel tried to finance an ever-growing 1997 budget shortfall with tax increases. On Sunday Gerhardt was more conciliatory.
He told Sunday's Frankfurter Allgemeine Sonntagszeitung paper he had spoken to Waigel "and we are agreed within the coalition to get down to spending cuts".
But Waigel's lieutenants in the Christian Social Union (CSU), Bavarian sister party of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), kept piling pressure on the FDP.
"The FDP has always chosen cabinet ministries where it never really had to prove it was prepared to make savings," CSU parliamentary leader Michael Glos told the news weekly Focus.

A shortfall of several billion marks for the 1997 budget has opened up deep rifts between the CDU/CSU and the shaky FDP, which sees the crisis as a threat to the tax-cutting image on which it has staked its political survival.

The CDU/CSU, caught between a pledge to meet the Maastricht budget criteria and fear of a backlash against radical state spending cuts, wants to keep its budget options open and suspects the FDP wants to play tax-cutter at its expense.

Waigel himself rounded on maverick FDP leader Juergen Moellemann, who has threatened that 12 FDP members from his North Rhine-Westphalia state will scupper the budget in parliament if they do not get a tax cut pledge for 1998.
"Even FDP deputies have a duty to the public good which includes solid state finances, not just tax cuts," he told the daily Bild, according to an advance release from Monday's paper.
Waigel is already struggling to find between three and four billion marks to cover a known budget gap for 1997.
But the news weekly Der Spiegel suggested the situation might be even worse for him.

It said federal and state tax experts would, when they meet on Thursday and Friday, reveal that 1997 tax revenue was set to fall 9 to 11 billion marks ($7.25 billion) short of expectations because of slow growth and high unemployment.
It said Waigel, who must present a balanced budget to the relevant parliamentary committee on November 14, would have to find six billion marks of this from federal funds.
Sunday's weekly Bild am Sonntag said tax revenue would be down three billion marks, and that two billion would have to come from Bonn.
The finance ministry declined to comment on the report before the experts' tax estimate was published.
Waigel is committed to avoiding new borrowing to fulfil the criteria for an EU single currency in 1999, leaving him no choice but to order new spending cuts -- or raise taxes.

Even as Gerhardt was saying the budget row was settled, he continued to insist that a two percentage point cut in an income tax surcharge -- put off from mid-1997 last month over furious FDP opposition -- would be implemented in full in 1998.
But Glos, backing Waigel's stated position, said the size of the cut was still open.
Bild am Sonntag said the coalition had weathered storms for so long that it was hard to imagine it might break up.
"But it is equally hard to imagine how the coalition is going to get through the next few weeks," it added.
